title: After a Major Decision, the Speed to Execution Matters
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post makes the case that once a major decision is made, the leader should move to execute within hours rather than days or weeks. Delay erodes the decision's relevance because it was based on yesterday's information, and in the meantime opportunities and team confidence slip away. The author warns against treating the announcement as a finish line, when it is really the starting line. Momentum is described as something the leader controls and everyone in the organization can sense. The piece is a brief argument for speed in follow-through, with no hedging on the point.
points: Slow execution undercuts the large investment of time and energy that went into the decision.
Because decisions rest on data that ages quickly, waiting for acceptance to settle is framed as a mistake.
A common leader error is to treat the decision itself as the hard part and the announcement as the end.
Without early momentum, real progress can take weeks or months to appear, so the leader is responsible for supplying the spark.
quotes: Good leaders act quickly to set the wheels of the team or organization in motion. They recognize that change is constant, and the decision was made with yesterday’s data, knowledge, and information. They seize the moment and the momentum to spring forward.
Waiting for the decision to settle or to be further accepted is a huge mistake. Major decisions need momentum to gain a fast hold and full traction.
The best leaders understand that they control this momentum and move to execute the decision hours later. Days and weeks do not cut it. There is simply no upside to waiting or delay.

In too many cases, leaders behave as if making the decision signals the finish line rather than the starting line. They conclude that the hard work has been completed, and all that is needed is for the decision to be announced and for the team to begin making preparations to act on it.

The momentum to execute any decision lies in the leader’s hands. The enthusiasm to move quickly is felt by everyone in the organization or not. Great leaders create the momentum to execute major decisions quickly.
